blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Aerial map matching provides position observations for navigation, but a position error alone does not determine how an observation should be weighted. We define five benchmark tasks: position availability and agreement, grouped error structure, predictive uncertainty, controlled updates, and temporal accumulation. A case study in digital-surface-model-assisted localization evaluates base-anchored uncertainty calibration within this framework. The method combines propagated image and map sensitivities with the second moment of a compact configuration subset relative to the reported position. The reported position remains unchanged, and scale is fitted using separate position references without local surface-height ground truth. Thirteen covariance models are evaluated on two held-out query sets from locations represented in the calibration data. Relative to a constant full-matrix baseline, the method reduces equal-location normalized position-update risk by 7.70% on 728 conditions and 5.46% on a separate 142 conditions under an independent prior, with all localization failures included. On the primary set, equal-location negative log likelihood improves by 2.571 nat. These results show improved reference-based weighting at seen locations. Exploratory base-quality and conditional-addition controls leave the incremental update benefit of configuration disagreement unresolved. Navigation benefit and real temporal accumulation remain untested.

blocks.en: I Introduction
blocks.zh: 一. 导言

blocks.en:
A position estimated by aerial image-to-map matching can correct navigation
drift. Assigning too much weight to an unreliable observation can degrade the
estimate, whereas assigning too little weight to an accurate observation
reduces the benefit of the correction. A digital surface model (DSM)
supplies localization geometry, with uncertainty in both matching and the map.
Average position error alone misses availability, persistent errors and whether
reported uncertainty leads to useful updates.

blocks.en: II Related Work
blocks.zh: 二. 相关工作

blocks.en:
Learned matchers such as SuperPoint–LightGlue, RoMa, and GIM-trained models
estimate image correspondences [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Our study addresses the subsequent estimation of horizontal position
uncertainty while holding a SIFT–DSM–PnP localizer fixed. This design
isolates uncertainty estimation rather than comparing matching systems.
OrthoLoC’s paired UAV–orthographic setting separates localization from
retrieval [ 8 ] , whereas AnyVisLoc examines a broader
retrieval–matching–DSM–pose pipeline [ 9 ] . We use the
paired setting, so the results concern localization within a supplied map region.

blocks.en: III Benchmark Definition
blocks.zh: 三. 基准定义

blocks.en:
The benchmark evaluates position observations through five questions:
availability and accuracy, error structure across groups, uncertainty
calibration, the effect of a controlled update, and error accumulation over time.
Controlled counterexamples in Fig. 2 illustrate
why these properties can differ despite identical aggregate position error.
Tasks and metrics are specified before comparing methods;
Table I lists the abbreviations.
The evaluation set contains N N predefined query conditions, termed
opportunities. Each completed attempt is classified as successful, failed or
rejected; unknown outcomes and unexecuted cases are recorded separately.
A successful output is a finite position. Each comparison specifies the
grouping, calibration/evaluation split, method versions, computational budget,
reference positions and covariance source (native, post-hoc or synthetic).
Calibration and evaluation sets are disjoint at the query level, with related
observations of each query assigned to the same set. Observations used during
method development are identified separately. Comparisons of uncertainty
models hold the position estimator and its computational budget fixed.

fallbacks and models use only calibration data.

blocks.en: VIII-C Limitations and Generalization
blocks.zh: 八-C 限制和概括

blocks.en:
All experiments share a reconstruction process. The main validation and
inPlace comparisons include only locations represented in calibration;
the location-held-out analyses remain part of method development.
Reference precision is unknown, map errors may be
correlated, and most configurations can agree on an incorrect position.
These factors limit generalization, and fitted scales should not be interpreted
as physical DSM-noise estimates. Because the positions are unchanged and
updates use an artificial independent prior, the results establish neither
improved localization accuracy nor navigation performance. Global retrieval,
temporal behavior and transfer require retrieval inputs, ordered flight
sequences and independently produced maps. The incremental value beyond H-Q
also needs evaluation at locations not used during method development.

blocks.en: VIII-D Conclusion
blocks.zh: 八-D 结论

blocks.en:
The benchmark links availability, error structure and predictive uncertainty
to the consequences of weighting position observations. In the case study,
base-anchored calibration improves predictive density and reduces the
prespecified equal-location update risk by 7.70% and 5.46% on two sets of
held-out queries at represented locations under a controlled independent prior.
These gains concern
reference-based weighting of unchanged positions. Exploratory H-Q and
conditional-addition comparisons leave the incremental update-risk benefit
of configuration disagreement unresolved. Independent-location evaluation
and ordered flight sequences are needed to assess transfer and navigation use.
